nodes.label: Large Language Models
nodes.desc: Neural networks trained on text to understand and generate language. Power ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini.

nodes.label: Transformers
nodes.desc: Architecture underlying all modern LLMs, using self-attention to process sequences in parallel.

learn.model: The architecture behind modern LLMs. Uses self-attention to process all tokens in parallel and capture long-range relationships.
learn.recallPrompt: Why did transformers replace RNNs for language? Name the key mechanism.
learn.doneWhen: You can explain self-attention and parallelism in your own words.

build.task: Run a pretrained transformer locally and inspect its attention or token outputs.
steps: Load a small model (e.g. via transformers lib)
build.doneWhen: You can show token-by-token output from a real model.

nodes.label: Embeddings
nodes.desc: Dense vector representations of meaning. Similar concepts produce vectors close together in space.

learn.model: Dense vectors that represent meaning. Similar concepts land close together, which powers search and RAG.
learn.recallPrompt: How does cosine similarity between embeddings represent semantic closeness?
learn.doneWhen: You can explain why embeddings enable semantic search.

build.task: Embed 10 sentences and find the two most similar by cosine similarity.
build.doneWhen: The closest pair is semantically sensible.

nodes.label: Tokenization
nodes.desc: How LLMs split text into sub-word units called tokens. Pricing is always per token.

learn.model: LLMs read text as tokens (sub-word units), not characters or words. Pricing and context limits are all measured in tokens.
learn.recallPrompt: Why is 'tokenization' the unit of both cost and context length?
learn.doneWhen: You can estimate token count for a paragraph and explain why it matters.

build.task: Tokenize three texts and compare token counts to word counts.
build.doneWhen: A small comparison of tokens vs words exists.

nodes.label: Context Window
nodes.desc: Maximum input length an LLM can process in a single call. Modern models: 128K to 2M tokens.

learn.model: The maximum amount of text (in tokens) a model can consider at once. Everything must fit: instructions, history, and retrieved data.
learn.recallPrompt: What happens when your input exceeds the context window?
learn.doneWhen: You can budget a prompt within a fixed context window.

build.task: Deliberately overflow a small context window and observe the failure, then fix it.
build.doneWhen: You demonstrate the overflow and a fix.

nodes.label: Fine-tuning
nodes.desc: Adapting a pre-trained model to a specific domain or task with additional training data.

nodes.label: RLHF
nodes.desc: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. Aligns model outputs to human preferences.

nodes.label: Foundation Models
nodes.desc: Large pre-trained models trained at scale, designed to be adapted to many downstream tasks.

nodes.label: Hallucination
nodes.desc: When LLMs generate plausible-sounding but factually incorrect content. Mitigated by RAG.

nodes.label: Prompt Engineering
nodes.desc: Designing effective inputs to get reliable, useful outputs from language models.

learn.model: Structuring the input to an LLM (instructions, examples, format) to reliably get the output you want.
learn.recallPrompt: List three techniques that improve prompt reliability.
learn.doneWhen: You can turn a vague prompt into a structured one with role, task, and format.

build.task: Take one weak prompt and improve it through three iterations, logging the difference.
build.doneWhen: You have a before/after that visibly improved.

nodes.label: RAG
nodes.desc: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: ground LLM answers in retrieved documents to reduce hallucination.

learn.model: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetch relevant documents and put them in the prompt so the model answers from your data, not just its training.
learn.recallPrompt: Draw the RAG pipeline: ingest, retrieve, augment, generate.
learn.doneWhen: You can explain why RAG reduces hallucination and when it fails.

build.task: Build a minimal RAG over five of your own documents.
steps: Stuff results into the prompt and answer
build.doneWhen: It answers a question using your documents.

nodes.label: Attention Mechanism
nodes.desc: Core mechanism in transformers that weighs how much each token should attend to every other token.

learn.model: The mechanism that lets a model weigh which other tokens matter for each token. Scaled dot-product attention is the core operation.
learn.recallPrompt: Write the attention formula and explain Q, K, V from memory.
learn.doneWhen: You can explain why attention is permutation-aware via positions.

build.task: Implement scaled dot-product attention in NumPy and visualize the weights.
build.doneWhen: You can show an attention heatmap.

nodes.label: Chain-of-Thought
nodes.desc: Prompting technique that makes the model reason step by step before producing an answer.

learn.model: Prompting the model to reason step by step before answering, which improves accuracy on multi-step problems.
learn.recallPrompt: Why does asking for steps improve reasoning accuracy?
learn.doneWhen: You can show a problem that fails without CoT and succeeds with it.

build.task: Find one reasoning task that fails direct, then fix it with chain-of-thought.
steps: Add 'think step by step' and compare
build.doneWhen: You have a fail and a fix side by side.

nodes.label: Inference
nodes.desc: Running a trained model to generate predictions or text. Separate from training.

learn.model: Running a trained model to get an output. The cost, latency, and token limits of inference shape every real application.
learn.recallPrompt: What is the difference between training and inference, and why does inference cost matter in production?
learn.doneWhen: You can explain why inference, not training, dominates most production AI bills.

build.task: Measure latency and token cost of one model across three prompt sizes.
steps: Make a tiny table comparing them
build.doneWhen: A 3-row table of latency and cost exists.

nodes.label: GPT-4o
nodes.desc: OpenAI flagship. Multimodal, 128K context. Most widely tested model in enterprise.

nodes.label: Claude 4
nodes.desc: Anthropic current generation: Haiku, Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.8, Fable 5. 200K context.

nodes.label: Gemini 2.0
nodes.desc: Google flagship. Up to 2M context window. Native multimodal including video.

nodes.label: Llama 3.x
nodes.desc: Meta open-weight family. 70B matches frontier models. Apache 2.0 license.

nodes.label: Mistral AI
nodes.desc: European LLM provider. Strong multilingual, EU data residency, competitive pricing.

nodes.label: DeepSeek
nodes.desc: DeepSeek V3 and R1. Benchmark performance matching GPT-4o at significantly lower cost.

nodes.label: Grok (xAI)
nodes.desc: Elon Musk's xAI model. Integrated with X platform data. Strong coding and STEM.

nodes.label: Qwen (Alibaba)
nodes.desc: Alibaba open-weight family. Strong Chinese and multilingual. Apache 2.0 license.

nodes.label: Reasoning Models
nodes.desc: o1, o3, o4-mini, DeepSeek R1: think before answering. Measurably better at math and logic.

nodes.label: AI Agents
nodes.desc: LLMs with tool access that can take actions, not just generate text. Observe, decide, act.

nodes.label: Multi-Agent Systems
nodes.desc: Multiple specialized agents collaborating on complex tasks. Each owns a capability.

nodes.label: LLM Gateway
nodes.desc: Central routing layer for multi-model, multi-provider LLM access. Adds fallback and cost control.

nodes.label: Microservices
nodes.desc: Small, independently deployable services that compose into a larger system.
nodes.invented: The term was popularized by James Lewis and Martin Fowler's article on 25 March 2014, building on a James Lewis talk in 2012.

sources.title: Microservices: a definition of this new architectural term (Lewis and Fowler, 2014)

nodes.label: APIs
nodes.desc: Interfaces that let services communicate and share data. The integration layer.

nodes.label: Vector Database
nodes.desc: Storage optimized for similarity search over embeddings. Core infrastructure for RAG.

nodes.label: Streaming Responses
nodes.desc: Token-by-token delivery of LLM responses. Reduces perceived latency for users.

nodes.label: Async Queues
nodes.desc: Background job processing for long-running AI tasks that exceed HTTP timeout limits.

nodes.label: Structured Output
nodes.desc: Constraining LLM output to valid JSON or typed schemas for reliable downstream use.

nodes.label: Claude API
nodes.desc: Anthropic API. Enterprise-focused, strong instruction following. 200K context.

nodes.label: Amazon Bedrock
nodes.desc: AWS managed LLM service. Multi-model access, data stays in your AWS account.

nodes.label: SageMaker
nodes.desc: AWS ML platform for training, hosting, and monitoring models at scale.

nodes.label: Supabase
nodes.desc: Open-source Firebase alternative. Includes pgvector for embedding storage and search.

nodes.label: FastAPI
nodes.desc: Python API framework. Async-first, auto-generates OpenAPI docs. Ideal for AI backends.

nodes.label: Railway
nodes.desc: Deployment platform with automatic CI/CD for backend services. No Kubernetes required.

nodes.label: Expo
nodes.desc: React Native framework for building iOS and Android apps from one codebase.

nodes.label: Stripe Connect
nodes.desc: Payment infrastructure for platforms and marketplaces with multi-party payouts.

nodes.label: Zustand
nodes.desc: Minimal React state management. No boilerplate, works with React hooks.

nodes.label: Zero-shot Prompting
nodes.desc: LLM tasks with no examples in the prompt. Relies entirely on pre-training knowledge.

nodes.label: Few-shot Learning
nodes.desc: Providing 2-5 examples in the prompt to guide output format and style.

learn.model: Giving the model a few examples in the prompt so it infers the pattern, with no fine-tuning.
learn.recallPrompt: When do few-shot examples help more than a longer instruction?
learn.doneWhen: You can convert a zero-shot prompt to a working few-shot one.

build.task: Build a classifier purely from 3 in-prompt examples.

nodes.label: ReAct Pattern
nodes.desc: Reason + Act loop: model thinks, calls tools, observes output, repeats until done.

nodes.label: Tool Use
nodes.desc: LLM ability to call external functions, APIs, and databases as part of generation.

nodes.label: Semantic Caching
nodes.desc: Cache LLM responses by semantic similarity to reduce cost and latency.

nodes.label: Chain Summarization
nodes.desc: Summarize long documents by processing chunks sequentially, combining results.

nodes.label: Chunking
nodes.desc: Splitting documents into segments before embedding and indexing for RAG.

learn.model: Splitting documents into pieces the right size for retrieval. Chunk too big and you lose precision; too small and you lose context.
learn.recallPrompt: What are the trade-offs of large vs small chunks in RAG?
learn.doneWhen: You can pick a chunk size and justify it for a document type.

build.task: Chunk one long document three ways and compare retrieval quality.
steps: Split by fixed size, by paragraph, by heading
Note which returns the best context
build.doneWhen: You can say which chunking won and why.

nodes.label: Reranking
nodes.desc: Second-pass scoring of retrieved documents before assembly into LLM context.

nodes.label: Cloud Computing
nodes.desc: On-demand compute, storage, and services over the internet. Pay for what you use.

nodes.label: Containers
nodes.desc: Portable, isolated application environments. Docker packages your app and dependencies.

nodes.label: Kubernetes
nodes.desc: Container orchestration for scaled AI inference workloads. Autoscaling and resilience.
nodes.invented: Joe Beda, Brendan Burns, Craig McLuckie and team at Google open-sourced Kubernetes in June 2014, drawing on lessons from Google's internal Borg system.
nodes.standardized: Donated to the CNCF in 2015 and graduated in 2018.

sources.title: From Google to the world: the Kubernetes origin story (Google Cloud Blog)

nodes.label: CI/CD
nodes.desc: Automated testing and deployment pipelines. Code merged to main triggers a deploy.

nodes.label: Observability
nodes.desc: Logging, metrics, and tracing for production AI systems. Catch regressions early.

nodes.label: Databases
nodes.desc: Structured data storage. Relational (Postgres), document (Mongo), vector (pgvector).

nodes.label: Serverless
nodes.desc: Function-as-a-service. Scales to zero, pay per invocation. AWS Lambda, Vercel Functions.

nodes.label: Version Control
nodes.desc: Tracking code changes over time. Git and GitHub are the industry standard.

nodes.label: EU AI Act
nodes.desc: EU regulation classifying AI by risk level. High-risk systems require conformity assessment.

nodes.label: ISO 42001
nodes.desc: International standard for AI management systems. Pairs with ISO 27001.

nodes.label: NIST AI RMF
nodes.desc: US framework for AI risk management: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage.

nodes.label: AI Safety
nodes.desc: Practices ensuring AI systems behave as intended without causing unintended harm.

nodes.label: Bias and Fairness
nodes.desc: Identifying and mitigating discriminatory patterns in training data and model outputs.

nodes.label: Data Governance
nodes.desc: Policies for data quality, lineage, ownership, and regulatory compliance.

nodes.label: OWASP LLM Top 10
nodes.desc: Security risks specific to LLM apps: prompt injection, insecure output handling, data leakage.

nodes.label: IBM Granite
nodes.desc: IBM open-source model. Apache 2.0, training data disclosed. Designed for regulated enterprise (finance, healthcare, legal).

nodes.label: OLMo (AllenAI)
nodes.desc: Allen Institute fully open model. Weights + training data + training code all public under Apache 2.0.

nodes.label: Falcon (TII)
nodes.desc: Technology Innovation Institute model. Apache 2.0 license. Strong Arabic-language capability.

nodes.label: StarCoder2
nodes.desc: BigCode code-generation model. 600+ programming languages. Permissive OpenRAIL-M license.

nodes.label: DBRX (Databricks)
nodes.desc: Databricks MoE model. 132B total, 36B active. Integrates natively with Databricks Lakehouse.

nodes.label: Groq
nodes.desc: Custom LPU hardware for LLM inference. 10-20x faster token generation than GPU. OpenAI-compatible API.

nodes.label: Together AI
nodes.desc: 100+ open-weight models on one API. Fine-tuning and custom model hosting. Largest open-model catalog.

nodes.label: Fireworks AI
nodes.desc: Inference provider with structured output support across all open models. FireOptimizer reduces cost.

nodes.label: Hugging Face
nodes.desc: Model hub with Inference API and Inference Endpoints. Thousands of community models available.

nodes.label: Ollama
nodes.desc: Run LLMs locally. OpenAI-compatible localhost API. Works on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs.

nodes.label: vLLM
nodes.desc: High-throughput open-source inference server. PagedAttention for efficient KV-cache. OpenAI-compatible.

nodes.label: Azure AI
nodes.desc: Microsoft managed AI platform. Azure OpenAI Service + AI Foundry + AI Search. Enterprise compliance certs.

nodes.label: Vertex AI
nodes.desc: Google Cloud managed ML platform. Model Garden (150+ models), Gemini access, pipeline tooling.

nodes.label: OCI Generative AI
nodes.desc: Oracle Cloud LLM service. AI Vector Search built into Oracle Database 23ai for in-database RAG.

nodes.label: Cursor
nodes.desc: AI code editor built on VS Code. Inline edits, codebase chat, and an agent mode for multi-file changes.

nodes.label: GitHub Copilot
nodes.desc: AI pair programmer inside the IDE. Autocomplete, chat, and agents across major editors.

nodes.label: Perplexity
nodes.desc: AI answer engine. Retrieval-augmented search that returns answers with cited sources.

nodes.label: Lovable
nodes.desc: Prompt-to-app builder. Generates full-stack web apps from natural-language instructions.

nodes.label: ElevenLabs
nodes.desc: AI voice synthesis and text-to-speech. Realistic voices, cloning, and dubbing.

nodes.label: Gamma
nodes.desc: AI presentation and document builder. Generates slide decks and pages from a prompt.

nodes.label: Stable Diffusion
nodes.desc: Open-weight image generation model. Runs locally, fine-tunable, with a large ecosystem.

nodes.label: ChatGPT
nodes.desc: OpenAI conversational assistant built on the GPT models. The product that mainstreamed LLMs.
nodes.invented: OpenAI released ChatGPT on 30 November 2022.

sources.title: Introducing ChatGPT (OpenAI, 2022)

nodes.label: Generative AI
nodes.desc: AI that creates new text, images, audio, or code rather than only classifying existing inputs.

learn.model: AI that creates new content (text, images, code) by learning patterns from huge datasets, rather than following hand-written rules.
learn.recallPrompt: Explain what makes a model 'generative' versus 'predictive', with one example of each.
learn.doneWhen: You can describe the input-to-output flow of a generative model without notes.

build.task: Call a hosted LLM API and make it generate three different formats from the same prompt.
steps: Send one prompt, print the response
Re-run asking for JSON, then a poem
build.doneWhen: A script runs end to end and prints three outputs.

nodes.label: Machine Learning
nodes.desc: Systems that learn patterns from data instead of being explicitly programmed rule by rule.

learn.model: Software that learns a mapping from examples instead of explicit rules. Training adjusts parameters to reduce error on data.
learn.recallPrompt: Describe supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning in one sentence each.
learn.doneWhen: You can explain how a model 'learns' from data to a non-technical person.

build.task: Train a tiny classifier on a toy dataset and measure its accuracy.
steps: Print accuracy on a held-out split
build.doneWhen: You can show a train/test accuracy number.

nodes.label: Neural Networks
nodes.desc: Layered networks of weighted nodes. The structure underneath deep learning and modern LLMs.

learn.model: Layers of weighted nodes that transform inputs into outputs. Stacking layers lets the network learn complex patterns.
learn.recallPrompt: Sketch a 2-layer network and explain what weights and activations do.
learn.doneWhen: You can describe forward pass and why non-linearity matters.

build.task: Implement a 2-layer neural net forward pass by hand in NumPy.
build.doneWhen: The forward pass returns the expected shape.

nodes.label: NLP
nodes.desc: Natural Language Processing: teaching machines to read, parse, and generate human language.

nodes.label: Computer Vision
nodes.desc: AI that interprets images and video. Detection, classification, and segmentation.

nodes.label: Vibe Coding
nodes.desc: Directing AI tools to build software through natural language instead of writing code by hand.

nodes.label: Agentic Loops
nodes.desc: The observe, plan, act, and reflect cycle that lets agents pursue goals over many steps.

learn.model: Letting an LLM plan, call tools, observe results, and repeat until a goal is met, instead of answering in one shot.
learn.recallPrompt: Describe the observe-think-act loop and where it can run away.
learn.doneWhen: You can explain why agents need stopping conditions and guardrails.

build.task: Build a tiny agent that uses one tool in a loop to answer a question.
steps: Define one tool (e.g. a calculator or search)
Let the model decide when to call it
build.doneWhen: The agent calls the tool and stops cleanly.

nodes.label: Agent Memory

nodes.label: Gartner Magic Quadrant
nodes.desc: How Gartner plots vendors on completeness of vision and ability to execute, and how to read it.
nodes.invented: Gideon Gartner founded the analyst firm Gartner in 1979. The Magic Quadrant visual research format emerged in the 1990s.
nodes.standardized: The Magic Quadrant became the most cited vendor-comparison format in enterprise IT buying.

sources.title: Magic Quadrant FAQ (Gartner official)

nodes.label: Gartner Hype Cycle
nodes.desc: The five stages from technology trigger to plateau of productivity, a lens for telling hype from durable value.
nodes.invented: Gartner analyst Jackie Fenn introduced the Hype Cycle in 1995 to describe the maturity pattern of emerging technologies.
nodes.standardized: Gartner publishes Hype Cycle reports across dozens of technology areas every year.

sources.title: Gartner Hype Cycle Research Methodology (Gartner official)

nodes.label: Abacus
nodes.desc: A manual counting frame that represents place values with beads or pebbles in columns. A person can add, subtract, multiply and divide by moving counters.
nodes.invented: Counting devices emerged in Sumer around 2700 to 2300 BCE. The Salamis Tablet (c. 300 BCE) is the oldest surviving counting board.
nodes.standardized: Settled into regional forms: the Roman hand-abacus, the Chinese suanpan and later the Japanese soroban.

sources.title: Salamis tablet, marble (Computer History Museum, CHM Revolution)

nodes.label: Pascaline (Pascal's calculator)
nodes.desc: A mechanical adding machine that used geared ten-tooth wheels to add and subtract, with carries propagated automatically. Multiplication and division were done by repeated addition.
nodes.invented: Blaise Pascal designed and built the Pascaline in 1642 in Rouen, France, to help with his father's tax accounting.
nodes.standardized: Pascal received a Royal Privilege in 1649 granting exclusive rights to make and sell the machine in France.
nodes.legal: Royal Privilege (a monopoly grant) issued to Pascal in 1649.

sources.title: Pascaline, Mechanical Calculator (Britannica)

nodes.label: Leibniz Step Reckoner
nodes.desc: A mechanical calculator using Leibniz's stepped drum and a movable carriage. It was the first machine that could perform all four arithmetic operations.
nodes.invented: Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz designed the Step Reckoner from around 1672, presenting a wooden model to the Royal Society, and completed working brass machines by 1694.
nodes.standardized: Leibniz's stepped-drum mechanism became a standard calculator design reused for the next 250 years.

sources.title: A Leibniz Stepped Reckoner calculator (Computer History Museum)

nodes.label: Jacquard loom (punched-card control)
nodes.desc: A loom controlled by a chain of punched cards, where holes in each card select which threads lift for each row. It automated complex patterned weaving.
nodes.invented: Joseph-Marie Jacquard developed his punched-card loom control in France around 1804, building on earlier punched designs by Vaucanson.
nodes.standardized: The chained-punched-card loom spread rapidly across the European textile industry and became the dominant pattern-weaving method.

sources.title: Joseph Marie Jacquard (IEEE Computer Society, Computer Pioneers)

nodes.label: Babbage's Analytical and Difference Engines
nodes.desc: The Analytical Engine was a design for a general-purpose, programmable mechanical computer with a processing mill, a memory store and punched-card input.
nodes.invented: Charles Babbage announced the Difference Engine in 1822 and began designing the general-purpose Analytical Engine from 1837 in London.
nodes.standardized: Never completed in his lifetime. The Science Museum London built a working Difference Engine No. 2 to his designs in 1991.

sources.title: Overview, The Babbage Engine (Computer History Museum)
Charles Babbage's Difference Engines (Science Museum London)

nodes.label: Ada Lovelace's algorithm (Note G)
nodes.desc: A step-by-step table of operations for the Analytical Engine that computes Bernoulli numbers using loops. It is widely regarded as the first published algorithm intended for a machine.
nodes.invented: Ada Lovelace published Note G, an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers on Babbage's Analytical Engine, in her 1843 translation of Menabrea's Sketch of the Analytical Engine.

sources.title: Menabrea, Sketch of the Analytical Engine, trans. A.A.L., Scientific Memoirs Vol. 3 (1843), Wikisource primary text

nodes.label: Boolean algebra
nodes.desc: A system of algebra in which variables take only the values true and false (1 and 0) and combine via AND, OR and NOT. It treats logic as a branch of mathematics.
nodes.invented: George Boole introduced his algebra of logic in The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) and developed it fully in An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (1854).
nodes.standardized: Became the formal basis of digital logic after Shannon applied it to switching circuits in 1937.

sources.title: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (George Boole, 1854), full text, Internet Archive
George Boole (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

nodes.label: Hollerith punched-card tabulator
nodes.desc: A system that recorded data as holes punched in cards, then counted and sorted the cards electromechanically. It cut the 1890 census tabulation from years to months.
nodes.invented: Herman Hollerith patented the electromechanical punched-card tabulator (US Patent 395,782, granted 1889) and used it to process the 1890 US Census.
nodes.standardized: Hollerith's company merged in 1911 and was renamed IBM in 1924. Punched cards became the dominant data medium for decades.
nodes.legal: US Patent 395,782, Art of Compiling Statistics, granted 1889.

sources.title: Herman Hollerith Receives a Patent (Computer History Museum, This Day in History)
Herman Hollerith and Mechanical Tabulation (US Census Bureau History)

nodes.label: Turing machine (On Computable Numbers)
nodes.desc: An abstract machine that reads and writes symbols on an infinite tape according to a finite table of rules. Turing used it to define which problems are computable.
nodes.invented: Alan Turing wrote On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem (received 28 May 1936), published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society.
nodes.standardized: The Turing machine became the standard formal model of computation, central to computability theory.

sources.title: A. M. Turing, On Computable Numbers, Proc. London Math. Soc. ser. 2 vol. 42 (1936-37), full text PDF

nodes.label: Shannon: switching logic and information theory
nodes.desc: Shannon's thesis showed electrical switching circuits can implement Boolean logic. His 1948 paper defined information mathematically, introduced the bit and set limits on reliable communication.
nodes.invented: Claude Shannon's 1937 MIT master's thesis applied Boolean algebra to relay and switching circuits. His 1948 paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication founded information theory.
nodes.standardized: The 1948 paper, in the Bell System Technical Journal, established information theory and the bit as the unit of information.

sources.title: C. E. Shannon, A symbolic analysis of relay and switching circuits (MIT thesis), DSpace@MIT
C. E. Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication, Bell System Technical Journal 27 (1948)

nodes.label: ENIAC
nodes.desc: A room-sized machine of about 17,468 vacuum tubes, the first general-purpose, electronic, programmable computer in the US. It computed artillery firing tables far faster than any earlier machine.
nodes.invented: J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly built ENIAC at the University of Pennsylvania's Moore School. It ran in 1945 and was unveiled on 14 February 1946.
nodes.standardized: It operated until 1955 and set the template for electronic computing.

sources.title: ENIAC (Penn Engineering, University of Pennsylvania)

nodes.label: von Neumann architecture (EDVAC report)
nodes.desc: A computer design in which both program instructions and data are held in the same read-write memory, processed by a single control unit and arithmetic unit. This is the stored-program concept.
nodes.invented: John von Neumann wrote the First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC, circulated 30 June 1945 at the Moore School, University of Pennsylvania.
nodes.standardized: The stored-program von Neumann architecture became the de facto standard organization for nearly all general-purpose computers since.

sources.title: John von Neumann, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (1945), full text, Internet Archive

nodes.label: Transistor
nodes.desc: A solid-state semiconductor device that amplifies or switches electrical signals. It replaced the bulky, hot, fragile vacuum tube.
nodes.invented: John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, in William Shockley's group at Bell Labs, demonstrated the first working point-contact transistor on 16 December 1947.
nodes.standardized: Announced 30 June 1948. The junction and silicon transistors made it the standard electronic switch by the late 1950s.
nodes.legal: US Patent 2,524,035 (filed 1948, issued 1950).

sources.title: 1947: Invention of the Point-Contact Transistor (Computer History Museum, The Silicon Engine)

nodes.label: UNIVAC I
nodes.desc: The first commercially produced electronic digital computer in the United States, built for business and government data processing. It used vacuum tubes and magnetic tape.
nodes.invented: Designed by Eckert and Mauchly (later Remington Rand). The first unit was accepted by the US Census Bureau in 1951.
nodes.standardized: Forty-six UNIVAC I machines were built. It established the commercial computer market.

sources.title: UNIVAC I (US Census Bureau History)

nodes.label: Magnetic-core memory
nodes.desc: Memory built from tiny magnetizable ferrite rings threaded on a grid of wires, each ring storing one bit by its magnetization. It gave fast, reliable, non-volatile random access.
nodes.invented: Jay Forrester at MIT developed coincident-current magnetic-core memory for Project Whirlwind, demonstrated in 1953.
nodes.standardized: Core memory was the dominant computer main memory through the 1950s and 1960s, until semiconductor RAM replaced it in the 1970s.
nodes.legal: Forrester patent US 2,736,880. IBM paid MIT a large settlement for rights in 1964.

sources.title: 1953: Whirlwind computer debuts core memory (Computer History Museum, The Storage Engine)

nodes.label: First compiler (Grace Hopper's A-0)
nodes.desc: The A-0 system translated symbolic code into machine code that UNIVAC could run. It was an early translator program, closer to a loader and linker than a modern compiler.
nodes.invented: Grace Hopper wrote the A-0 system for UNIVAC I in 1951 to 1952 and described automatic programming in her 1952 ACM paper The Education of a Computer.
nodes.standardized: Recognized as an IEEE Milestone. The compiler idea led to FLOW-MATIC, FORTRAN and COBOL.

sources.title: Grace Hopper, The Education of a Computer, Proceedings of the 1952 ACM National Meeting (ACM Digital Library)

nodes.label: FORTRAN
nodes.desc: FORTRAN (FORmula TRANslation) was the first widely used high-level programming language, aimed at scientific and engineering calculation. Its compiler produced efficient machine code from algebra-like statements.
nodes.invented: John Backus's team at IBM developed FORTRAN for the IBM 704. The reference manual is dated 1956 and the system shipped to customers in April 1957.
nodes.standardized: First standardized by ASA (later ANSI) in 1966, with later ISO standards.

sources.title: FORTRAN (Computer History Museum Software Preservation, original IBM documents)

nodes.label: Integrated circuit
nodes.desc: A single chip of semiconductor that holds many interconnected components formed together. It replaced wiring discrete parts by hand.
nodes.invented: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first working integrated circuit in 1958. Robert Noyce at Fairchild independently devised the practical monolithic silicon IC, filing his patent in 1959.
nodes.standardized: Monolithic silicon ICs became the universal basis of microelectronics in the 1960s.
nodes.legal: Kilby (TI) and Noyce (Fairchild) patents, followed by years of dispute and cross-licensing.

sources.title: 1959: Practical Monolithic Integrated Circuit Concept Patented (Computer History Museum)

nodes.label: COBOL
nodes.desc: COBOL (COmmon Business-Oriented Language) is a high-level language for business data processing, using English-like syntax so programs read like prose.
nodes.invented: COBOL was defined by the CODASYL committee, convened by the US Department of Defense in 1959. Grace Hopper's FLOW-MATIC heavily influenced its design.
nodes.standardized: The COBOL-60 specifications were approved in 1960 and published by the US Government. Later standardized by ANSI (1968) and ISO.

sources.title: COBOL: Initial Specifications for a Common Business Oriented Language (CODASYL, 1960), bitsavers scan

nodes.label: IBM System/360
nodes.desc: The first family of computers built to share one architecture and software across many machine sizes. A program written for a small model ran on a large one without rewriting.
nodes.invented: IBM announced the System/360 on 7 April 1964, the first family of computers built to share one architecture across a full range of machine sizes.
nodes.standardized: Its instruction-set architecture became a long-lived standard. IBM Z mainframes continue the lineage today.

sources.title: The IBM System/360 (IBM official history)
IBM Announces System/360 Computer Family (Computer History Museum)

nodes.label: Moore's law
nodes.desc: Moore observed that the number of components on an integrated circuit was doubling at a regular pace. The observation guided the semiconductor industry for decades.
nodes.invented: Gordon Moore, Cramming more components onto integrated circuits, Electronics magazine, 19 April 1965.

sources.title: Cramming more components onto integrated circuits (Computer History Museum catalog of the original article)

nodes.label: ARPANET
nodes.desc: The first operational packet-switched computer network and the direct ancestor of the internet. Its first message was sent between UCLA and SRI in 1969.
nodes.invented: The first host-to-host message was sent on 29 October 1969 from UCLA to SRI. The login attempt crashed after two characters, so the first text transmitted was lo.
nodes.standardized: Operational through the 1970s and 1980s, decommissioned in 1990 once its lineage was absorbed into the TCP/IP internet.

sources.title: Leonard Kleinrock, UCLA: The Day the Infant Internet Uttered its First Words (IMP Log primary record)

nodes.label: Unix
nodes.desc: A multi-user, multitasking operating system created at Bell Labs in 1969. Its file system, process model and pipelined commands shaped almost every operating system that followed.
nodes.invented: Development began in 1969 at Bell Labs (Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie and others) on a PDP-7. The first edition manual came in 1971.
nodes.standardized: POSIX (from 1988) and the Single UNIX Specification (from 1994) later standardized Unix interfaces.

sources.title: The Evolution of the Unix Time-sharing System (Dennis M. Ritchie, AT&T Bell Labs Technical Journal, 1984)

nodes.label: Relational model of data
nodes.desc: The relational model represents data as tables of tuples, separating the logical view of data from its physical storage. It gave databases a rigorous mathematical foundation.
nodes.invented: Edgar F. Codd, IBM Research San Jose, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks, Communications of the ACM, June 1970.

sources.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (E. F. Codd, CACM 13(6), June 1970)

nodes.label: Intel 4004 microprocessor
nodes.desc: The first commercial general-purpose programmable microprocessor, packing a complete 4-bit CPU onto a single chip. It was built for a calculator but designed to be reprogrammable.
nodes.invented: Intel announced the 4004 on 15 November 1971, developed with Busicom. It was the first commercial general-purpose programmable microprocessor, a whole 4-bit CPU on one chip.

sources.title: The First Programmable Microprocessor: The 4004 (Intel official timeline)

nodes.label: Networked email with @
nodes.desc: Networked email let a user on one computer send a message to a user on a different computer over the ARPANET. Tomlinson introduced the @ sign in 1971 to address mail across machines.
nodes.invented: Ray Tomlinson at BBN developed ARPANET's first network email in 1971 by combining SNDMSG and CPYNET, and chose the @ sign to separate user name from host name.
nodes.standardized: The user@host convention was later formalized in internet mail RFCs (RFC 821 and 822 in 1982).

sources.title: Official Biography, Raymond Tomlinson (Internet Hall of Fame)

nodes.label: C programming language
nodes.desc: A compiled, statically typed systems programming language created at Bell Labs to rewrite Unix. It gives low-level access to memory while staying portable across hardware.
nodes.invented: Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs evolved C from B between 1969 and 1973, with the most creative period in 1972, to build utilities and the Unix kernel.
nodes.standardized: Ratified as ANSI C (C89) in 1989 and adopted by ISO as C90 in 1990. ISO revisions continue (C99, C11, C17, C23).

sources.title: The Development of the C Language (Dennis M. Ritchie, Bell Labs)

nodes.label: Ethernet
nodes.desc: A local area network technology that lets computers share a broadcast medium using carrier sense multiple access with collision detection. It became the dominant standard for wired LANs.
nodes.invented: Robert Metcalfe and David Boggs created Ethernet at Xerox PARC. Metcalfe's foundational memo dates to 1973, and the CACM paper was published in 1976.
nodes.standardized: Patented as US 4,063,220 (issued 1977). Later standardized as IEEE 802.3 in 1983.
nodes.legal: US Patent 4,063,220 (assignee Xerox), issued 1977.

sources.title: Metcalfe & Boggs, Ethernet: Distributed Packet Switching for Local Computer Networks, CACM 19(7), July 1976
US Patent 4,063,220A (Google Patents)

nodes.label: TCP/IP
nodes.desc: The protocol suite that lets independent packet networks interconnect into a single internet. Cerf and Kahn described it in 1974, and ARPANET switched to it in 1983.
nodes.invented: Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn, A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, IEEE Transactions on Communications, May 1974.
nodes.standardized: On 1 January 1983, ARPANET conducted a coordinated flag-day cutover from NCP to TCP/IP, making it the mandatory standard.

sources.title: Cerf & Kahn, A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication, IEEE Trans. Communications, May 1974 (PDF)

nodes.label: SQL
nodes.desc: A declarative query language for relational databases that lets you describe what data you want rather than how to fetch it. It originated as SEQUEL at IBM.
nodes.invented: Donald Chamberlin and Raymond Boyce at IBM Research, SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language, 1974. SEQUEL was later renamed SQL for trademark reasons.
nodes.standardized: First standardized by ANSI in 1986 and ISO in 1987 (ISO 9075). Revised many times since.

sources.title: SEQUEL: A Structured English Query Language (Chamberlin & Boyce, 1974), IBM Research

nodes.label: SAP and enterprise resource planning
nodes.desc: SAP builds integrated, real-time business software that runs finance, supply chain, HR and operations from one connected data model. R/3 (1992) became the dominant ERP suite.
nodes.invented: Founded in 1972 in Germany by five former IBM engineers to build integrated, real-time business software.
nodes.standardized: The mainframe suite R/2 followed in 1979, and the three-tier client-server suite R/3 launched in 1992, setting the global standard for ERP.

sources.title: SAP History (SAP official company history)
SAP R/3 (release 1992, three-tier client-server ERP)

nodes.label: Oracle Database
nodes.desc: Oracle V2 (1979) was the first commercial SQL relational database. There was no shipped V1; the founders named the first release Version 2 so buyers would not distrust a first release.
nodes.invented: Larry Ellison, Bob Miner and Ed Oates released Oracle V2 in 1979, the first commercially available SQL-based relational database.

sources.title: Introduction to Oracle Database, History (Oracle official documentation)

nodes.label: IBM Personal Computer (5150)
nodes.desc: IBM's first mass-market personal computer. Its open architecture and published documentation let third parties build compatible machines, creating the IBM-compatible PC.
nodes.invented: IBM's Boca Raton team introduced the Personal Computer model 5150 on 12 August 1981, built on the Intel 8088 with an open architecture and off-the-shelf parts.
nodes.standardized: Its open, documented architecture let third parties build compatible hardware and software, creating the PC standard.

sources.title: IBM Introduces Personal Computer (Computer History Museum, This Day in History)
The IBM PC (IBM official history)

nodes.label: MS-DOS
nodes.desc: Microsoft's disk operating system for x86 PCs, shipped in 1981 with the original IBM PC. It gave users a command-line interface to manage files and run programs from floppy disks.
nodes.invented: Microsoft derived MS-DOS from 86-DOS (originally QDOS by Tim Paterson). It shipped with the IBM PC as PC DOS 1.0 in 1981.

sources.title: Microsoft MS-DOS early source code (Computer History Museum)

nodes.label: Graphical user interface (Apple Macintosh)
nodes.desc: The first commercially successful personal computer built around a graphical user interface and mouse. It brought windows, icons and point-and-click to a mass-market audience.
nodes.invented: The Apple Macintosh launched on 24 January 1984. The GUI lineage traces to the Xerox Alto (1973) and the commercial Xerox Star (1981) from Xerox PARC.

sources.title: A Computer for the Rest of Us (Computer History Museum)
50 Years Later, We're Still Living in the Xerox Alto's World (IEEE Spectrum)

nodes.label: Domain Name System (DNS)
nodes.desc: The distributed directory of the internet that translates names like example.com into the numeric IP addresses computers use. It uses a tree-structured namespace of name servers.
nodes.invented: Designed by Paul Mockapetris (USC ISI) and specified in RFC 882 and RFC 883, both November 1983, to replace the central HOSTS.TXT file with a distributed hierarchy.
nodes.standardized: RFC 882 and 883 (1983) were obsoleted by RFC 1034 and 1035 in 1987, which remain the base DNS standard.

sources.title: RFC 882: Domain names, Concepts and facilities (Mockapetris, 1983)
RFC 1034: Domain Names, Concepts and Facilities (1987, obsoletes 882)

nodes.label: GNU Project and the GPL
nodes.desc: The GNU Project builds a complete free operating system, and the GPL is the copyleft license that protects the freedom to use, study, modify and share that software.
nodes.invented: Richard Stallman announced the GNU Project on 27 September 1983, aiming to build a complete free Unix-compatible operating system.
nodes.standardized: GNU General Public License version 1 was published in February 1989, formalizing the copyleft model.
nodes.legal: GPLv1 (1989) introduced copyleft: anyone may use, modify and redistribute, but distributed derivative works must stay under the same license and ship their source.

sources.title: GNU Initial Announcement (Richard Stallman, 1983), gnu.org
GNU General Public License, Version 1 (1989), gnu.org

nodes.label: Microsoft Windows
nodes.desc: A graphical operating environment that ran on top of MS-DOS, adding windows, a mouse-driven interface and bundled programs. It grew into the dominant desktop operating system.
nodes.invented: Microsoft released Windows 1.0 on 20 November 1985 as a graphical shell running on top of MS-DOS.

sources.title: Microsoft Windows 1.01 (1985), Internet Archive (release date 1985-11-20)

nodes.label: World Wide Web
nodes.desc: The system of interlinked hypertext documents, identified by URLs and served over HTTP, that runs on top of the internet. It turned the internet into a global information space anyone could browse.
nodes.invented: Tim Berners-Lee wrote Information Management: A Proposal at CERN in March 1989. The first server and browser ran by the end of 1990, and the web went public in 1991.
nodes.standardized: CERN released the web software into the public domain on 30 April 1993. The W3C was founded in 1994 to develop open standards.
nodes.legal: CERN placed the web code in the public domain on 30 April 1993, relinquishing all rights to it.

sources.title: Tim Berners-Lee, Information Management: A Proposal (CERN, 1989), W3C archive
A short history of the Web (CERN)

nodes.label: Linux kernel
nodes.desc: A free, Unix-like operating system kernel that manages hardware and provides core services. It started as a hobby project and now runs most servers, cloud infrastructure and Android phones.
nodes.invented: Linus Torvalds announced the project on 25 August 1991 in the comp.os.minix newsgroup. Version 0.01 was released in September 1991.
nodes.standardized: Distributed under the GNU GPL from 1992. Developed openly at kernel.org to this day.
nodes.legal: Licensed under the GNU GPL version 2.

sources.title: Linus Torvalds, What would you like to see most in minix? comp.os.minix, 25 August 1991 (Google Groups archive)

nodes.label: Three-tier architecture
nodes.desc: Splits an application into three independent layers: a presentation tier for the interface, an application tier for business logic, and a data tier for storage.
nodes.invented: Emerged in the early 1990s as the dominant pattern for client-server applications, separating presentation, application logic and data tiers.
nodes.standardized: Never formally standardized. It became an industry convention through vendor middleware and technical literature.

sources.title: What Is Three-Tier Architecture? (IBM Think)

nodes.label: HTTP and HTML
nodes.desc: HTTP is the request-response protocol browsers use to fetch resources, and HTML is the markup language that structures web pages. Together they made the web work.
nodes.invented: Tim Berners-Lee invented HTTP and HTML at CERN around 1989 to 1991 to publish and link documents over the internet.
nodes.standardized: HTTP/1.0 documented in RFC 1945 (1996); HTTP/1.1 in RFC 2068 (1997, later RFC 2616).

sources.title: RFC 1945: Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP/1.0
RFC 2068: Hypertext Transfer Protocol, HTTP/1.1

nodes.label: Mosaic and Netscape Navigator
nodes.desc: Mosaic was the first widely used graphical web browser, putting images and text on the same page. Netscape Navigator commercialized that and drove early mass adoption.
nodes.invented: NCSA Mosaic was released in 1993 by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina. Andreessen co-founded Netscape, which shipped Navigator in late 1994.

sources.title: NCSA Mosaic (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Apache HTTP Server
nodes.desc: Open-source web server software that delivers web pages to browsers over HTTP. It became the most-used web server within a year of release.
nodes.invented: The Apache Group released its first public version in April 1995, building on the NCSA HTTPd server, and shipped Apache 1.0 on 1 December 1995.
nodes.legal: Apache License (open source).

sources.title: About the Apache HTTP Server Project (httpd.apache.org)

nodes.label: MySQL
nodes.desc: An open-source relational database that stores and queries structured data using SQL. It became the database half of the LAMP stack behind countless web apps.
nodes.invented: Michael Widenius and David Axmark released the first internal version of MySQL on 23 May 1995 at the Swedish company TcX.
nodes.legal: Dual-licensed GPL and commercial. Owned by Oracle since 2010.

sources.title: MySQL Retrospective: The Early Years (Oracle blog)

nodes.label: PHP
nodes.desc: A server-side scripting language designed to embed code in HTML and build dynamic web pages. It originally stood for Personal Home Page Tools.
nodes.invented: Rasmus Lerdorf announced Personal Home Page Tools 1.0 on 8 June 1995 and released its source code that month.
nodes.legal: PHP License (open source).

sources.title: History of PHP (official PHP manual)

nodes.label: Java
nodes.desc: A general-purpose language that compiles to bytecode and runs on the Java Virtual Machine, promising write once, run anywhere. It became a backbone of enterprise software.
nodes.invented: Sun Microsystems publicly introduced Java (created by James Gosling's team, originally named Oak) on 23 May 1995. JDK 1.0 shipped in January 1996.
nodes.legal: Owned by Oracle via the Sun acquisition. OpenJDK is GPL-licensed.

sources.title: Java (programming language) (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: JavaScript
nodes.desc: The scripting language that runs in web browsers to make pages interactive. It later spread to servers, tooling and almost every part of software development.
nodes.invented: Brendan Eich created the first prototype in about ten days in May 1995 at Netscape. It shipped in Navigator 2.0 and was renamed JavaScript in December 1995.
nodes.standardized: Standardized as ECMAScript by Ecma International (ECMA-262), first edition June 1997.

sources.title: Brendan Eich (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: SSL and TLS
nodes.desc: SSL and its successor TLS encrypt traffic between browsers and servers, enabling HTTPS. They provide confidentiality and server authentication for web communication.
nodes.invented: Netscape's Taher Elgamal designed SSL in 1994. SSL 2.0 shipped in 1995 and SSL 3.0 was finalized in November 1996.
nodes.standardized: The IETF standardized the protocol as TLS 1.0 in RFC 2246 (1999). SSL 3.0 was later documented in RFC 6101.

sources.title: RFC 2246: The TLS Protocol Version 1.0

nodes.label: Adobe (Macromedia) Flash
nodes.desc: A platform for animation, interactive content and video that ran via a browser plugin. It dominated rich web media in the 2000s before mobile and open standards displaced it.
nodes.invented: Macromedia acquired FutureSplash in December 1996 and rebranded it Macromedia Flash 1.0. Adobe acquired Macromedia in 2005.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Adobe ended Flash Player support on 31 December 2020 and blocked content in January 2021.

sources.title: Adobe Flash Player End of Life (Adobe)

nodes.label: XML 1.0
nodes.desc: A text format for marking up structured data so machines and people can both read it. It became the common format for config files, documents and web service messages.
nodes.invented: A W3C working group designed XML as a simplified subset of SGML for structured data exchange.
nodes.standardized: Published as a W3C Recommendation on 10 February 1998.

sources.title: Extensible Markup Language (XML) 1.0 (W3C Recommendation, 1998)

nodes.label: Salesforce and Software-as-a-Service
nodes.desc: Salesforce delivered enterprise CRM entirely over the web on a subscription, pioneering the Software-as-a-Service model. Customers paid per user instead of buying and installing software.
nodes.invented: Marc Benioff and co-founders started Salesforce in 1999 to deliver CRM as a browser-based subscription, branded No Software.
nodes.legal: Proprietary subscription (SaaS) model.

sources.title: The History of Salesforce (Salesforce News)

nodes.label: VMware x86 virtualization
nodes.desc: A bare-metal hypervisor that runs many isolated virtual machines on one physical x86 server. It let one machine safely host many operating systems.
nodes.invented: VMware, founded in 1998, shipped VMware Workstation in 1999 and the bare-metal ESX Server hypervisor in 2001, the first commercially successful x86 virtualization.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. After Broadcom's 2023 acquisition, VMware ended perpetual licenses and moved to subscription-only bundles, sharply raising costs. See broadcom-vmware.

sources.title: VMware (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: SOAP and web services
nodes.desc: An XML-based protocol for calling functions on remote servers over a network, the foundation of early enterprise web services. It wrapped requests in strict XML envelopes.
nodes.invented: Dave Winer's XML-RPC (1998) led to SOAP, developed with Microsoft, IBM and others.
nodes.standardized: SOAP 1.1 was published as a W3C Note in 2000. SOAP 1.2 became a W3C Recommendation in 2003.

sources.title: Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) 1.1 (W3C Note, 2000)

nodes.label: REST architectural style
nodes.desc: An architectural style that uses standard HTTP methods and resource URLs to build web APIs. It favors statelessness and simple, uniform interfaces over heavy protocols.
nodes.invented: Roy Fielding defined REST in Chapter 5 of his 2000 PhD dissertation at the University of California, Irvine.
nodes.standardized: Described in an academic dissertation rather than a formal standard, but widely adopted as the dominant web API style.

sources.title: Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures (Fielding, 2000)

nodes.label: Windows XP
nodes.desc: Microsoft's consumer and business desktop operating system, known for stability and a long life. Many machines, including ATMs and industrial systems, still run it years after support ended.
nodes.invented: Microsoft released Windows XP to general availability on 25 October 2001.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Mainstream support ended in 2009, extended support ended on 8 April 2014.

sources.title: Windows XP (Microsoft Lifecycle)

nodes.label: Manifesto for Agile Software Development
nodes.desc: A short statement of values favoring working software, collaboration and responding to change over rigid plans and processes. It reframed how teams build software.
nodes.invented: Seventeen software practitioners met at Snowbird, Utah in February 2001 and wrote the Agile Manifesto, defining four values and twelve principles.

sources.title: Manifesto for Agile Software Development

nodes.label: Dynatrace and APM
nodes.desc: An application performance monitoring and observability platform that traces transactions across distributed systems. It helps teams find and fix performance problems in production.
nodes.invented: Bernd Greifeneder and co-founders started Dynatrace in Linz, Austria in 2005 to trace application performance end to end.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Publicly traded on the NYSE since 2019.

sources.title: Dynatrace, Bernd Greifeneder (LinzWiki)

nodes.label: Google Reader
nodes.desc: A web-based RSS and Atom feed aggregator that let people follow blogs and news in one place. Its shutdown became a landmark example of a beloved product being killed.
nodes.invented: Google launched Reader through Google Labs on 7 October 2005.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Shut down on 1 July 2013.

sources.title: A second spring of cleaning (Google official blog, announcing the shutdown)

nodes.label: Git
nodes.desc: A distributed version control system that tracks changes to source code and lets many developers work in parallel. Every clone holds the full project history.
nodes.invented: Linus Torvalds wrote Git in April 2005 after the Linux kernel project lost free access to the proprietary BitKeeper tool.
nodes.legal: GPLv2 (open source).

sources.title: Git turns 20: A Q&A with Linus Torvalds (GitHub Blog)

nodes.label: Amazon S3
nodes.desc: Cloud object storage where developers store and retrieve any amount of data over the internet, paying only for what they use. It was the first widely adopted AWS service.
nodes.invented: AWS launched Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) on 14 March 2006, offering scalable object storage over a web services API.
nodes.legal: Proprietary, usage-based pricing.

sources.title: Amazon Web Services Launches (Amazon press release, 2006)

nodes.label: Amazon EC2
nodes.desc: On-demand virtual servers in the cloud that you can launch and shut down in minutes, paying by the hour. It removed the need to buy physical hardware upfront.
nodes.invented: AWS announced Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) as a public beta on 25 August 2006, providing resizable virtual servers built on Xen.
nodes.legal: Proprietary, usage-based pricing.

sources.title: Amazon EC2 Beta (AWS News Blog, 2006)

nodes.label: The term cloud computing
nodes.desc: Cloud computing is the idea that data and applications live on remote servers accessed over the internet rather than on local machines. The phrase entered mainstream use in 2006.
nodes.invented: Google CEO Eric Schmidt used cloud computing to describe a server-based service model at a conference on 9 August 2006, popularizing the term.

sources.title: Who Coined Cloud Computing? (MIT Technology Review)

nodes.label: Apache Hadoop
nodes.desc: An open-source framework for storing and processing huge datasets across clusters of commodity machines. It brought distributed big-data processing to the masses.
nodes.invented: Doug Cutting and Mike Cafarella split Hadoop out of the Nutch project in early 2006, inspired by Google's GFS and MapReduce papers.
nodes.legal: Apache License (open source).

sources.title: Apache Hadoop (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Apple iPhone
nodes.desc: Combined a phone, music player and internet device with a multi-touch screen into one product. It launched the modern smartphone and the mobile-first era.
nodes.invented: Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone on 9 January 2007. It went on sale in the US on 29 June 2007.
nodes.legal: Proprietary.

sources.title: Apple Reinvents the Phone with iPhone (Apple Newsroom, 2007)

nodes.label: Heroku
nodes.desc: A platform-as-a-service that lets developers deploy apps with a git push, without managing servers. It popularized the developer-friendly PaaS model.
nodes.invented: Founded in 2007. Heroku launched commercially with Ruby support in 2009 and was acquired by Salesforce in 2010.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Owned by Salesforce since 2011.

sources.title: Salesforce.com Completes Acquisition of Heroku (Salesforce)

nodes.label: GitHub
nodes.desc: A hosting platform for Git repositories with collaboration features like pull requests and issues. It became the center of open-source and team software development.
nodes.invented: Tom Preston-Werner, Chris Wanstrath and PJ Hyett launched GitHub publicly on 10 April 2008.
nodes.legal: Proprietary. Owned by Microsoft since 2018.

sources.title: We Launched (GitHub Blog, April 2008)

nodes.label: Android
nodes.desc: An open-source, Linux-based mobile operating system led by Google and the Open Handset Alliance. It became the world's most widely used mobile platform.
nodes.invented: Google and the Open Handset Alliance announced Android on 5 November 2007. The first Android phone, the HTC Dream, shipped in October 2008.
nodes.legal: Open source (Apache License) with proprietary Google services on top.

sources.title: Industry Leaders Announce Open Platform for Mobile Devices (Open Handset Alliance)

nodes.label: Google App Engine
nodes.desc: A platform-as-a-service that runs web apps on Google's infrastructure with automatic scaling. Developers upload code and Google handles the servers.
nodes.invented: Google launched App Engine as a developer preview on 7 April 2008, initially supporting Python.
nodes.legal: Proprietary, usage-based pricing.

sources.title: Introducing Google App Engine (Google App Engine Blog, 2008)

nodes.label: Node.js
nodes.desc: A runtime that lets JavaScript run on servers using a non-blocking, event-driven model. It made JavaScript a full-stack language.
nodes.invented: Ryan Dahl created Node.js in 2009, pairing Google's V8 engine with an event loop for server-side JavaScript, and presented it at JSConf EU in November 2009.
nodes.legal: Open source. Governed by the OpenJS Foundation.

sources.title: Node.js (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: MongoDB
nodes.desc: A document-oriented NoSQL database that stores data as flexible JSON-like documents instead of rigid tables. It suits rapidly changing schemas and large-scale web apps.
nodes.invented: 10gen (now MongoDB Inc.) open-sourced MongoDB in February 2009 as a document-oriented NoSQL database.
nodes.legal: Originally AGPL v3, relicensed to the source-available SSPL in 2018. See mongodb-sspl.

sources.title: MongoDB (Wikipedia)

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.desc: An in-memory key-value data store used as a database, cache and message broker. Its speed and simple data structures made it a standard caching layer.
nodes.invented: Salvatore Sanfilippo created Redis in 2009 to scale his startup, open-sourcing the first public release in April 2009.
nodes.legal: Originally BSD. Later relicensed (RSALv2 and SSPL in 2024, with an AGPL option added in 2025).

sources.title: Thank You, Salvatore Sanfilippo (Redis blog)

nodes.label: Microsoft Azure
nodes.desc: A public cloud platform offering compute, storage, databases and many managed services. It is one of the three dominant global cloud providers.
nodes.invented: Microsoft unveiled Windows Azure on 27 October 2008. It reached general availability on 1 February 2010.
nodes.legal: Proprietary, usage-based pricing.

sources.title: Windows Azure General Availability (Official Microsoft Blog, 2010)

nodes.label: OpenStack
nodes.desc: An open-source platform for building and running private and public clouds, providing compute, storage and networking. It aimed to be an open alternative to proprietary clouds.
nodes.invented: Rackspace and NASA announced OpenStack in July 2010. The first release, code-named Austin, shipped in October 2010.
nodes.legal: Apache License. Governed by the Open Infrastructure Foundation.

sources.title: Announcing the OpenStack 2010.1 Austin Release (OpenStack Blog)

nodes.label: DevOps
nodes.desc: A culture and practice that merges software development and IT operations to ship changes faster and more reliably. Debois named it when he organized the first devopsdays in 2009.
nodes.invented: The term was coined by Patrick Debois for the first devopsdays conference in Ghent, October 2009.

sources.title: The Incredible True Story of How DevOps Got Its Name (New Relic)

nodes.label: Apache Kafka
nodes.desc: A distributed event-streaming and publish-subscribe system built at LinkedIn to track high-volume activity events. It became the default backbone for real-time data pipelines.
nodes.invented: Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede and Jun Rao built Kafka at LinkedIn and open-sourced it in January 2011.
nodes.standardized: Became an Apache Software Foundation top-level project in 2012.

sources.title: Open-sourcing Kafka, LinkedIn's distributed message queue (LinkedIn blog, 2011)

nodes.label: React
nodes.desc: A JavaScript library for building user interfaces from composable components with a virtual DOM. Facebook open-sourced it in 2013, and it became the dominant front-end library.
nodes.invented: Jordan Walke at Facebook created React. It was unveiled at JSConf US in May 2013 and introduced on the React blog in June 2013.

sources.title: Why did we build React? (React blog, June 2013)

nodes.label: Docker
nodes.desc: Docker packages an application and its dependencies into a portable container image that runs the same anywhere. It made Linux containers easy enough for mainstream developers.
nodes.invented: Solomon Hykes at dotCloud demoed Docker at PyCon on 13 March 2013 and open-sourced it under Apache 2.0.
nodes.standardized: The image and runtime format were later standardized via the Open Container Initiative (2015).

sources.title: The Docker project turns 10 (Snyk retrospective on the 2013 PyCon launch)

nodes.label: Terraform
nodes.desc: An infrastructure-as-code tool that provisions cloud and on-prem resources from declarative configuration files. It pioneered cloud-agnostic, declarative provisioning.
nodes.invented: Mitchell Hashimoto and Armon Dadgar at HashiCorp announced Terraform on 28 July 2014.
nodes.legal: Open source under MPL 2.0 until 2023, when HashiCorp relicensed it to the source-available BSL. See hashicorp-bsl and opentofu.

sources.title: HashiCorp Terraform announcement (HashiCorp blog, 2014)

nodes.label: AWS Lambda and serverless
nodes.desc: Runs code in response to events without provisioning or managing servers, billing only for execution time. It launched the mainstream serverless computing model.
nodes.invented: AWS announced Lambda at re:Invent on 13 November 2014.

sources.title: AWS Lambda, Run Code in the Cloud (AWS News Blog, 2014)

nodes.label: Cloud Native Computing Foundation
nodes.desc: A Linux Foundation body that hosts and governs cloud-native open-source projects, starting with Kubernetes. It provides vendor-neutral stewardship for the ecosystem.
nodes.invented: Founded under the Linux Foundation on 21 June 2015, with Kubernetes as the seed project.

sources.title: Cloud Native Computing Foundation (official site)

nodes.label: TensorFlow
nodes.desc: Google's open-source machine learning framework for building and training neural networks. Its 2015 release made large-scale deep learning broadly accessible.
nodes.invented: Google Brain open-sourced TensorFlow in November 2015.

sources.title: TensorFlow, Google's latest machine learning system, open sourced for everyone (Google Open Source Blog, 2015)

nodes.label: GraphQL
nodes.desc: A query language and runtime for APIs that lets clients request exactly the data they need in one round trip. Facebook built it in 2012 and released it publicly in 2015.
nodes.invented: Lee Byron, Nick Schrock and team at Facebook built GraphQL internally in 2012 and released the public spec in September 2015.
nodes.standardized: The GraphQL Foundation (Linux Foundation) was formed in 2018, and the spec is maintained openly.

sources.title: GraphQL: a data query language (Engineering at Meta, 2015)

nodes.label: Site Reliability Engineering
nodes.desc: SRE applies software engineering practices to operations, using error budgets and service-level objectives to balance reliability and feature velocity.
nodes.invented: The practice was started by Ben Treynor Sloss at Google in 2003 and codified in the O'Reilly book Site Reliability Engineering in 2016.
nodes.standardized: Defined as a discipline by the 2016 Google SRE book.

sources.title: Google SRE book, Part I Introduction (states SRE began at Google in 2003)

nodes.label: Transformer architecture
nodes.desc: A neural network architecture based entirely on attention, dispensing with recurrence and convolution. It became the foundation of nearly all modern large language models.
nodes.invented: Vaswani et al. at Google, Attention Is All You Need, published on arXiv on 12 June 2017.

sources.title: Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani et al., arXiv:1706.03762, 2017)

nodes.label: Service mesh (Istio)
nodes.desc: An infrastructure layer that handles traffic management, security and observability between microservices without changing application code. Istio popularized the pattern in 2017.
nodes.invented: Istio was launched by Google, IBM and Lyft, built on Lyft's Envoy proxy, on 24 May 2017.

sources.title: Introducing Istio: the first public release (Istio.io, 2017)

nodes.label: Python 2 end of life
nodes.desc: Python 2 reached end of life on 1 January 2020, after which it received no further fixes, security patches or improvements. It capped a long migration to Python 3 begun in 2008.
nodes.invented: The Python Software Foundation sunset Python 2 on 1 January 2020.

sources.title: Sunsetting Python 2 (Python.org)

nodes.label: GPT-3
nodes.desc: OpenAI's 175-billion-parameter language model that performs tasks from few-shot prompts without fine-tuning. It showed that scaling Transformers produced broad general capability.
nodes.invented: OpenAI published Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (Brown et al.) on arXiv on 28 May 2020.

sources.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners (Brown et al., arXiv:2005.14165, 2020)

nodes.label: SolarWinds supply-chain compromise
nodes.desc: Attackers inserted a backdoor into SolarWinds Orion software updates, compromising US government agencies and many enterprises. It is a landmark software supply-chain attack.
nodes.invented: The compromise was disclosed publicly in December 2020. CISA issued Emergency Directive 21-01 on 13 December 2020.

sources.title: Advisory AA20-352A (CISA, 17 December 2020)

nodes.label: Red Hat shifts CentOS to CentOS Stream
nodes.desc: Red Hat ended CentOS Linux, a free rebuild of RHEL, and refocused on CentOS Stream, an upstream branch that tracks ahead of RHEL. CentOS Linux 8 support was cut from 2029 to the end of 2021.
nodes.invented: Red Hat announced the shift on 8 December 2020.
nodes.legal: Not a license change but a drastic support and lifecycle change. The shortened lifecycle (2029 cut to 2021) angered users and spawned the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux forks.

sources.title: CentOS Project shifts focus to CentOS Stream (Blog.CentOS.org, 2020)

nodes.label: Kubernetes removes dockershim
nodes.desc: Kubernetes deprecated and later removed dockershim, the shim that let the kubelet talk to Docker, in favor of CRI-compliant runtimes like containerd. Docker-built images keep working.
nodes.invented: Deprecation was announced for Kubernetes v1.20 on 2 December 2020. dockershim was removed in v1.24, released in May 2022.

sources.title: Don't Panic: Kubernetes and Docker (Kubernetes blog, 2020)

nodes.label: MongoDB relicenses to SSPL
nodes.desc: MongoDB moved its Community Server from the AGPLv3 open-source license to its own SSPL in 2018, targeting cloud providers offering MongoDB as a managed service.
nodes.invented: MongoDB issued the Server Side Public License (SSPL) on 16 October 2018.
nodes.legal: SSPL is source-available but not OSI-approved open source. It requires anyone offering the software as a service to open-source their entire service stack, which is impractical for cloud providers. The OSI rejected SSPL as open source.

sources.title: MongoDB Issues New Server Side Public License (MongoDB press release, 2018)

nodes.label: Elastic relicenses Elasticsearch
nodes.desc: Elastic moved Elasticsearch and Kibana from the Apache 2.0 open-source license to dual SSPL and the Elastic License. The move targeted Amazon's managed Elasticsearch service.
nodes.invented: Elastic announced the change on 14 January 2021.
nodes.legal: Moved from OSI-approved Apache 2.0 to SSPL and Elastic License 2.0, neither OSI open source. AWS forked the last Apache-2.0 versions into OpenSearch. Elastic re-added an AGPLv3 option in 2024.

sources.title: Doubling down on open, Part II (Elastic blog, 2021)

nodes.label: Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228)
nodes.desc: A critical remote code execution flaw (CVSS 10.0) in the ubiquitous Apache Log4j 2 logging library, exploitable via crafted log strings. It affected countless Java applications worldwide.
nodes.invented: A critical flaw in Apache Log4j 2, reported to Apache in November 2021 and publicly disclosed on 9 December 2021.

nodes.label: HashiCorp relicenses to BSL
nodes.desc: HashiCorp moved Terraform, Vault, Consul and other products from the MPL 2.0 open-source license to the Business Source License (BSL). The change restricts competitive commercial use and triggered the OpenTofu fork.
nodes.invented: HashiCorp announced adoption of the Business Source License v1.1 on 10 August 2023.
nodes.legal: Moved from OSI-approved MPL 2.0 to BSL/BUSL 1.1, which is source-available, not OSI open source. The BSL forbids using the code to offer a competing product. Each version converts to MPL 2.0 four years after release.

sources.title: HashiCorp adopts Business Source License (HashiCorp blog, 2023)

nodes.label: OpenTofu (Terraform fork)
nodes.desc: The community-driven, MPL-2.0 open-source fork of Terraform created after HashiCorp's BSL relicensing. It is drop-in compatible and governed neutrally under the Linux Foundation.
nodes.invented: A community fork of Terraform. The OpenTF manifesto appeared on 15 August 2023, and the project joined the Linux Foundation as OpenTofu on 20 September 2023.
nodes.standardized: Governed by the Linux Foundation.
nodes.legal: Preserves the original MPL 2.0 open-source license that Terraform abandoned. A direct response to the HashiCorp BSL change, forked from the last MPL-2.0 release.

sources.title: Linux Foundation Launches OpenTofu (Linux Foundation press release, 2023)

nodes.label: Broadcom acquires VMware
nodes.desc: Broadcom closed its acquisition of VMware in 2023, then ended perpetual licenses weeks later and moved VMware to subscription-only bundles. It reshaped enterprise virtualization economics.
nodes.invented: Broadcom completed its roughly 69 billion dollar acquisition of VMware on 22 November 2023, then ended perpetual licensing on 11 December 2023.
nodes.legal: A major commercial licensing change. On 11 December 2023 VMware ended sale of perpetual licenses, moving to subscription or term licenses only and bundling products. Existing customers must convert to subscription at renewal.

sources.title: Broadcom Completes Acquisition of VMware (Broadcom investor relations, 2023)
VMware End of Availability of Perpetual Licensing (VMware blog, 2023)

nodes.label: Frontier models (GPT-4 and Claude)
nodes.desc: In March 2023, OpenAI released the multimodal GPT-4 and Anthropic launched Claude on the same day, opening the era of competing frontier large language models.
nodes.invented: OpenAI announced GPT-4 and Anthropic launched Claude on the same day, 14 March 2023.

sources.title: GPT-4 (OpenAI, 2023)
Introducing Claude (Anthropic, 2023)

nodes.label: AI agents and agentic systems
nodes.desc: AI agents wrap large language models with tools, memory and planning so they can pursue multi-step goals. AutoGPT's 2023 release sparked broad interest in agentic systems.
nodes.invented: The wave began in 2023 to 2024. AutoGPT, released on 30 March 2023, sparked broad interest in autonomous agents.

sources.title: AutoGPT repository (Significant-Gravitas, GitHub)

paths.label: AI Engineer
paths.desc: A balanced path from AI foundations to building real applications.

eras.driver: Calculation was done by hand or by gears. Each device automated one more step of arithmetic or logic, building the ideas that electronic computers would later run.
eras.name: Pre-electronic computing

eras.driver: Vacuum tubes and then the transistor let machines compute with electricity instead of moving parts. Computing went from one-off lab experiments to the first commercial machines.
eras.name: The electronic dawn

eras.driver: Computers were rare, huge and expensive, so one central machine served many users. Shared architectures, the first networks and the relational database appeared.
eras.name: The mainframe era

eras.driver: Cheap microprocessors put a computer on every desk. Work moved off the central machine, and open standards let independent vendors build a whole ecosystem.
eras.name: PC and client-server

eras.driver: The web connected personal computers to the entire world. Browsers, open-source servers and the first internet businesses defined the dot-com era.
eras.name: The web and enterprise

eras.driver: Renting computing by the hour replaced buying servers. Amazon, Google and Microsoft turned infrastructure into a utility, and the smartphone put it in every pocket.
eras.name: The cloud era

eras.driver: Containers and orchestration made software portable and elastic. Teams adopted DevOps, microservices and automation to ship continuously at scale.
eras.name: Cloud-native and DevOps

eras.driver: Transformer models turned data into general capability, while a wave of open-source relicensing and vendor consolidation reminded everyone that IT is contracts as much as code.
eras.name: AI-native and the license wars
